opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, it's great to be here.

I think the biggest change has been a shift in mindset more than any single result. For a long time, robotics was this world of very specialized systems: you'd build one pipeline for grasping, another for navigation, hand-engineer the perception, tune everything for one lab, one robot, one task. Over the past year or so, the field has really embraced the idea that robots can benefit from the same recipe that worked for language and vision. That means large, pretrained models, lots of diverse data, and a single policy that can do many things instead of one.

Concretely, you see that in vision-language-action models, where you take a model that already understands images and text from the internet and teach it to output robot actions. What's exciting is that the robot inherits some of that world knowledge. You can ask it to do something it never saw in its robot training data, like "move the object to the picture of the country where this food comes from," and it can sometimes reason through it, because that semantic understanding came from the web.

The second big change is data. People now see data collection as the central bottleneck and are treating it seriously: teleoperation at scale, pooling datasets across many institutions and many different robot bodies, and finding that training across embodiments actually helps rather than hurts. That was not obvious a few years ago.

And third, there's been a huge influx of capital and talent, especially around humanoids and general-purpose robots. Some of that is hype, honestly. We're still far from robots that are reliable enough to deploy everywhere, and the last mile of robustness is really hard. But the overall direction, toward generalist robot foundation models, feels like a real inflection point.

r001.rationale: The response describes a move toward generalist robot models, but does not identify a shift from academic tabletop demonstrations to realistic deployment settings.

r002.rationale: It mentions increased capital and says robots are not yet reliable enough for broad deployment, but does not connect commercial interest to higher robustness requirements.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that tabletop demonstrations once considered impressive have become mundane.

r004.rationale: It mentions an influx of capital but says nothing about investment affecting how openly the state of the art is shared.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest change is that robotics finally stopped being bottlenecked on the brain and started being bottlenecked on the body and the data. For a long time, the hard part was the policy: how do you get a robot to understand what you mean, generalize to a new object, recover when something goes slightly wrong. And what we've seen is that the same recipe that worked for language, big pretrained models, lots of diverse data, instruction following, actually transfers. Vision-language-action models went from a research curiosity to something that multiple labs can train, and you can hand one a novel task in a kitchen it's never seen and get a reasonable attempt rather than nothing.

That changes the character of the field. Two or three years ago, a demo meant one robot, one task, hundreds of hours of tuning. Now the interesting question is how fast you can collect enough real-world episodes, across enough embodiments, to keep that generalization curve going. So you see this shift in where the money and the talent go: teleoperation farms, simulation pipelines, cross-embodiment datasets, hardware that's cheap enough to deploy in the hundreds rather than the single digits. Humanoids are part of that story, not because the form factor is magic, but because it's a bet that one body in a human-built world lets you reuse data and models across tasks instead of building a bespoke machine for every one.

The other thing I'd flag is that the gap between a good video and a reliable product is still enormous, and I think the past year made people more honest about that. Ninety percent success looks incredible in a clip and is unusable in a warehouse. So the maturation I'm most excited about is less the headline capabilities and more that the field is starting to talk seriously about reliability, evaluation, safety, and what it actually takes to run these systems for thousands of hours without a human babysitting. That's the part that will decide whether this is a real revolution or another hype cycle.

r001.rationale: Contrasts earlier one-robot demos with collecting real-world episodes and deploying hardware at scale, including warehouse use.

r002.rationale: Links shifting money and talent toward robotics deployment with the need for reliability over long operating periods.

r003.rationale: It contrasts earlier demos with newer capabilities, but never says demonstrations that seemed impressive a year ago have become mundane.

r004.rationale: It discusses investment and talent shifts but says nothing about how commercialization affects openness in sharing the state of the art.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change is the shift from building a robot policy for one specific task to building generalist models that can learn across many tasks. Instead of starting from scratch every time you want a robot to do something new, you’re trying to build on capabilities it already has.

That changes how we think about data, too. An experience collected on one task could help with another task. The question becomes: how do we get that transfer to work reliably, across different environments and potentially different robots?

There’s still a big gap between a compelling demonstration and a robot that works consistently in someone’s home. But I think the exciting change is that we’re increasingly approaching robotics as a problem of learning broadly from experience, rather than engineering each behavior individually.

r002.rationale: It notes a gap between demonstrations and reliable home use, but does not connect commercialization to higher robustness requirements.

r003.rationale: It does not say that tabletop demonstrations once considered impressive have become mundane.

r004.rationale: It does not mention commercial investment or changes in how openly robotics advances are shared.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest change is the shift toward more general-purpose robot learning. Instead of building a separate system for every task, we’re moving toward models that can use language and visual input to perform a range of behaviors.

That changes the question we’re asking. It’s less, “Can we get a robot to do this one thing?” and more, “What can it transfer from things it’s already learned, and how much new experience does it need?” Reliability is still the hard part—getting something to work once is very different from having it work consistently in a new environment. But that shift toward generalization is what I find most exciting.

r002.rationale: It says reliability is difficult, but does not connect increased commercialization interest to higher robustness requirements.
